content: Percodan is a powerful combination painkiller designed to manage moderate to severe acute pain. It contains two active ingredients: aspirin, a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), and oxycodone, a potent opioid agonist. Oxycodone is a semi-synthetic opioid derived from thebaine, an alkaloid found in opium, although thebaine itself has no therapeutic value. Oxycodone is metabolized into oxymorphone and is known for its high oral bioavailability, making it effective when taken by mouth. Unlike morphine, oxycodone has a longer half-life and better oral potency, which contributed to its widespread use in the past. Each Percodan tablet contains 4.5 mg of oxycodone hydrochloride, 0.38 mg of oxycodone terephthalate, and 325 mg of aspirin. The inactive ingredients include FD&C Yellow 10, FD&C Yellow 6, microcrystalline cellulose, and starch. Historically, Percodan also contained a small amount of caffeine. The standard dosage is one tablet every six hours as needed for pain, with a maximum daily limit of 12 tablets. Percodan was first introduced in the United States in 1950 by DuPont Pharmaceuticals and was once one of the most commonly prescribed painkillers. However, its use has significantly declined over the years. This decline is largely due to the development of alternative oxycodone-based medications, such as Percocet, which combines oxycodone with acetaminophen (Tylenol) instead of aspirin. Aspirin, as an anti-inflammatory agent, can increase prothrombin time and impair blood clotting, which poses a risk of excessive bleeding in post-operative patients. As a result, Percocet and other oxycodone-containing drugs have become more popular for managing post-operative pain. Additionally, hydrocodone-based medications like Norco and Vicodin, which combine hydrocodone with acetaminophen, have gained favor because hydrocodone is nearly as effective as oxycodone but is less strictly regulated. In the United States, Percodan is classified as a Schedule II controlled substance under the Uniform Controlled Substances Act of 1970, placing it in the same category as cocaine, morphine, and raw opium. Schedule II drugs are subject to strict regulations, including a prohibition on refills and restrictions on telephone prescriptions, except in emergencies. In contrast, hydrocodone-containing medications like Vicodin and Norco were previously classified as Schedule III substances, which are less tightly regulated (though hydrocodone was reclassified to Schedule II in 2014). These regulatory differences, along with the availability of alternative medications, have contributed to the decline in Percodan prescriptions since the 1960s. Percodan is also marketed under the brand name Endodan and is currently manufactured by Endo Pharmaceuticals. Like all oxycodone-containing products, Percodan carries a significant risk of abuse and dependence. Oxycodone can lead to addiction similar to that caused by morphine, making it a drug of choice for individuals with opioid use disorder. However, many opioid users prefer OxyContin, a formulation of oxycodone that does not contain additional active ingredients like aspirin (in Percodan) or acetaminophen (in Percocet).
